title: Race, Income, and Neighborhood Safety: Diminished Returns of Income Among Non-Hispanic Black Americans
content: Background. According to marginalization-related diminished returns (MDRs) theory, socioeconomic resources tend to buy less health and less advantage for Black than for White Americans. Neighborhood safety may even be one of the mechanisms linking higher SES to better health, but Black–White differences in its SES gradient are not well described. Objective. To test whether the associations of education, income, and employment with a safe neighborhood differ between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White adults. Methods. We used the 2025 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (n = 84,616 adults, 4,937 non-Hispanic Black and 79,679 non-Hispanic White, in the 19 jurisdictions that asked about neighborhood safety). The outcome was rating the neighborhood as safe or extremely safe from crime (versus unsafe or extremely unsafe). Exposures were a college degree, household income of $50,000 or more, and being employed versus out of work. We fitted weighted models fully interacted with race, adjusted for age and sex, and read the Black–White difference in the SES association on the additive and ratio scales. Sensitivity analyses used mutual adjustment for the three indicators, an outcome of extremely safe, and the reverse coding (unsafe). We report uncorrected p-values. Results. Non-Hispanic Black adults reported a safe neighborhood less often than non-Hispanic White adults (90.2% vs 96.8%; p < .001). A college degree was associated with a larger gain in safety for non-Hispanic Black adults (+9.3 points) than for non-Hispanic White adults (+1.4; difference 7.9, p < .001), and the ratio was also larger (p < .001). Income showed no Black–White difference in the main model (5.7 vs 4.3 points; p = .410), but a smaller return for non-Hispanic Black adults appeared when education and employment were held constant (0.2 vs 5.4 points; difference −5.3, p = .049) and on the ratio scale for living in an unsafe neighborhood (ratio 1.76, p = .010). Being employed was associated with a similar gain in neighborhood safety in Black and non-Hispanic White adults (p = .192 for the difference between them). Conclusions. The data did not show a consistent diminished return of SES on neighborhood safety for non-Hispanic Black adults. Unexpectedly, and contrary to MDR theory, a college degree was more strongly associated with neighborhood safety among non-Hispanic Black than among non-Hispanic White adults. A smaller return of income appeared only in some specifications and is offered as a hypothesis for replication.
